paragraphs: Rav Yitzchak bar Chinena or Chanina.

He was a disciple of Rav Huna. In [Ketubot 4b](https://www.sefaria.org/Ketubot.4b.3): Rabbi Yitzchak bar Ch. speaks in the name of Rav Huna. Hyman counts three statements transmitted by R’ Yitzchak bar Chanina in the name of Rav Huna at Ketubot 61b.[^4] [Berakhot 52b](https://www.sefaria.org/Berakhot.52b.22) has Rabbi Yosi son of R’ Chanina speaking in the name of Rav Huna. Hyman says the name should read R' Yitzchak bar Ch., as in the Rif and Dikdukei Soferim there, note yod. [Nedarim 38b](https://www.sefaria.org/Nedarim.38b.2) has Rav Yitzchak bar Chanania speaking in the name of Rav Huna. [Sanhedrin 38b](https://www.sefaria.org/Sanhedrin.38b.2) has Rabbi Yochanan son of R' Chanina; Seder HaDorot suggests that it should perhaps read R' Yitzchak bar Ch., while Dikdukei Soferim there reads R' Chama bar Ch.[^1]

notes.text: Chinena and Chanina represent Hyman’s two heading forms. Where he abbreviates the patronymic ב״ח or בר״ח, “bar Ch.” retains that abbreviation. His definite correction in Berakhot differs from Seder HaDorot’s “perhaps” in Sanhedrin. The Rif and Dikdukei Soferim readings are cited as Hyman reports them; “note yod” is the lettered note.

The Davidson text calls him Rabbi Yitzchak at Ketubot 4b:3, but Rav Yitzchak at Nedarim 38b:2. Berakhot has Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina, while Sanhedrin has Rabbi Yochanan bar Chanina; Hyman discusses competing readings of these names.
We did not locate that threefold attribution in the consulted Ketubot 61b text. The count remains Hyman’s report.
In the consulted [Ketubot 61a:9-12](https://www.sefaria.org/Ketubot.61a.9-12), Rav Yitzchak bar Chananya speaks three times in Rav Huna’s name. Hyman gives 61b and the form Chanina in this notice.
